mcqs.question: Why does inserting into a heap append the new value at the end of the array rather than somewhere else?
options: Because that's the only position that keeps the tree complete before sift-up runs
Because the end of the array is always where the maximum value belongs
Because sift-up requires the new value to start at the root
Because appending avoids ever needing to sift-up at all
mcqs.explanation: The next open array slot is exactly the next leaf position a complete tree would fill, so appending there preserves completeness immediately; sift-up then only has to fix ordering, not shape. Sift-up almost always runs after an insert — it's rarely skippable.

mcqs.question: When extracting the root of a min-heap, why move the last array element into the root's slot instead of promoting one of the root's children?
options: Because the last element is always the second-smallest value
Because promoting a child would require sifting up instead of down
Because moving the last element keeps the tree complete, matching how insert appends at the last slot
Because children can't be moved without breaking the array indices
mcqs.explanation: The last element occupies the last leaf, so removing it from there and placing it at the root keeps the tree complete — the mirror image of insert's append-at-the-end. Promoting a child directly would leave a hole at that child's old position and break completeness.

mcqs.question: A sift-down implementation unconditionally compares a node against both `heap[left]` and `heap[right]` without checking array bounds first. What's the risk?
options: It will always throw an index-out-of-range error immediately
Nothing — every complete binary tree guarantees both children exist
It runs correctly but with worse time complexity
For a node with only one child (or no children), it can compare against a stale or out-of-bounds index and silently produce an invalid heap
mcqs.explanation: The last level of a complete tree can stop partway through, so a node can legitimately have zero, one, or two children — sift-down must bounds-check each child index before comparing. Skipping the check doesn't always crash; depending on the language it can read stale data and corrupt the heap without raising an error.

mcqs.question: Build-heap calls sift-down starting from index (n // 2) - 1 down to 0. Why skip the indices above (n // 2) - 1?
options: Those indices are leaves with no children, so they're already trivially valid one-node heaps
Those indices belong to a different, unrelated subtree
Skipping them is an optimization that trades correctness for speed
Those indices are processed separately by sift-up instead
mcqs.explanation: Every index past (n // 2) - 1 is a leaf in a complete tree of size n, and a leaf alone already satisfies the heap property trivially. Build-heap only needs to fix internal nodes, working bottom-up so each node's children are already valid heaps by the time it's processed.

mcqs.question: Build-heap calls sift-down on roughly n/2 nodes, each potentially costing O(log n) in the worst case, yet the total is O(n). What resolves the apparent contradiction?
options: Most of those n/2 calls are on nodes near the bottom of the tree, whose maximum possible sift-down cost is small — the per-node costs form a geometric series that sums to O(n)
Sift-down is actually O(1) amortized when called on internal nodes only
The n/2 estimate is wrong; build-heap only ever calls sift-down on O(log n) nodes
Build-heap uses sift-up instead of sift-down internally, which is cheaper
mcqs.explanation: The O(log n)-per-call bound is a worst case reached only by nodes near the root, and there are exponentially fewer of those; summing (count at each height) times (max cost at that height) is a geometric series that converges to O(n), not O(n log n). This is the standard proof, not a different algorithm or a wrong node count.

mcqs.question: After heap sort finishes sorting an array in place, is the array still a valid heap?
options: Yes, because sift-down is always called at the very end to restore it
No — the repeated root-swap-and-shrink sequence leaves the array in sorted order, which generally violates the heap property
Yes, sorted order is a special case of heap order
It depends on whether the array was a min-heap or max-heap to start
mcqs.explanation: Heap sort consumes the heap to produce a sorted array; the final array is sorted, not heap-ordered, since a sorted ascending array (for a max-heap sort) has the smallest element at the root, violating the max-heap property everywhere. If you need a live heap afterward, you must rebuild it separately.
